title: Why Ergonomics in Manufacturing Should Be a Focus — MSC Industrial Supply Co.
summary: Learn how to reduce ergonomic injuries and fatigue-related near-misses with practical, low-cost interventions that work. Here’s what you need to know.
body_markdown:
Bending, twisting, turning and lifting heavy objects are common body movements for manufacturing workers, and the toll adds up fast. They can result in painful injuries and, sometimes, costly periods of time away from work for recovery.


An injury related to this kind of work is called a musculoskeletal disorder (or MSD), also referred to as an ergonomic injury. It occurs when your body “uses muscles, tendons and ligaments to perform tasks, oftentimes in awkward positions or in frequent activities, which over time can create pain and injury,”[according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/iif/factsheets/msds.htm) (BLS).


MSDs remain one of the most common and costliest categories of workplace injury. According to the[National Safety Council’s analysis of BLS data](https://injuryfacts.nsc.org/work/safety-topics/musculoskeletal-injuries/) , the private sector logged nearly 938,000 MSD cases involving days away from work, job restriction or transfer in 2023-24 alone. Disabling workplace injuries[cost U.S. businesses more than $59 billion annually](https://www.mscdirect.com/knowledge-center/articles/understanding-cost-workplace-injuries-and-how-prevent-them) .


An effective ergonomics program reduces the risk of injury to workers while maintaining or improving their health. The idea is to design the job to fit the worker, not physically forcing the worker’s body to fit the job.


But workstation design tells only part of the story.


## The Link Between Ergonomics and Fatigue


Traditional ergonomics programs treat body mechanics and worker fatigue as separate concerns—one addressed through workstation design, the other through break schedules or wellness initiatives. But on a 24/7 production floor, the two are inseparable.


In facilities that run multiple shifts—particularly second and third shift or rotating schedules—fatigue itself becomes an ergonomic hazard, changing how workers move and react.


[Research on cyclic lifting tasks](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12923468/) has found that as trunk and limb muscles fatigue, workers change their lifting posture and mechanics in ways that increase peak spinal forces—the body compensating for tired muscles by shifting the work elsewhere. Reaction time and judgment slip, too: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)[notes](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2020/fatigue-work.html) that staying awake for 17 consecutive hours produces performance impairment comparable to a blood alcohol content of 0.05 percent.


## Ergonomic Risk Factors on the Manufacturing Floor


Industrial ergonomic workstations are created to accommodate workers and adapt to their physical attributes rather than forcing a worker to adapt to the work environment.


Using a poorly designed workstation or completing a task using an improper method can put a worker at risk of injury. Common ergonomic risk factors on a production floor include repetitive motion, excessive exertion, and awkward or static postures.


By arranging work environments in a way that follows the body’s natural movements, potential injuries may be reduced, prevented or eliminated.


## How Shift Work and Rotating Schedules Compound Fatigue Risk


Manufacturing plants that run multiple shifts or rotation schedules face a fatigue risk that single-shift daytime operations don’t. Working against the body’s natural circadian rhythm disrupts sleep quality and duration.


[According to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration](https://www.osha.gov/worker-fatigue/hazards) (OSHA), accident and injury rates are 18 percent greater during evening shifts and 30 percent greater during night shifts compared with day shifts, and working 12-hour shifts increases the risk of injury by 37 percent.


Rotating schedules add to the problem, since workers rarely get enough time to fully adjust before their schedule changes again. So do extended shifts and overtime:[NIOSH’s review of overtime research](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/11308) found that the ninth through 12th hours of a shift bring measurably reduced alertness, slower cognition and more errors.


## Warning Signs: When Fatigue Becomes a Safety Hazard


Fatigue shows up in the body before it shows up on an incident report—and in more than one way. According to[OSHA](https://www.osha.gov/worker-fatigue/hazards) , fatigue can cause “weariness, sleepiness, irritability, reduced alertness, impaired decision-making, and lack of motivation, concentration and memory.” That list spans both physical and cognitive symptoms, and both deserve equal attention on the floor.


Physical warning signs include heavy eyelids, yawning, slower or clumsier movements, and workers who start fumbling tools or tasks they normally handle smoothly. Cognitive warning signs include trouble concentrating and remembering, and sleepiness on the job.


***Read more:***[5 Minute Safety Talk: Ergonomics](https://www.mscdirect.com/knowledge-center/articles/5-minute-safety-talk-ergonomics)


## Ergonomic Interventions That Reduce MSDs


The most effective ergonomics programs consider the risks faced by each worker at their workstation. In the past, this has been achieved by hiring ergonomics experts to assess workplaces and train employees, but many companies don’t have the budget for it. Thankfully, simple, low-cost solutions are often available.


For example, dynamic shelving, storage and picking solutions bring items from a storage area to the production, assembly or packing station, ensuring that workers don’t have to fetch and carry needed parts.[Organizer bins](https://www.mscdirect.com/browse/tn?navid=2109609&searchterm=bins) that minimize clutter around workstations and[floor mats](https://www.mscdirect.com/browse/tn?navid=2106389&searchterm=floor+mats) that reduce worker fatigue after long periods of standing also help to improve safety by reducing the possibility of injuries.


As OSHA[notes](https://www.osha.gov/ergonomics/control-hazards) , many industries have successfully implemented ergonomic solutions to minimize MSD injury risks by “modifying existing equipment, making changes in work practices, and purchasing new tools or other devices to assist in the production process.” OSHA says these changes have “reduced physical demands, eliminated unnecessary movements, lowered injury rates and their associated workers’ compensation costs, and reduced employee turnover.”


***Read more:***[How Using Automation in Facilities Helps to Reduce Workplace Injuries](https://www.mscdirect.com/knowledge-center/articles/how-using-automation-facilities-helps-reduce-workplace-injuries)


For facilities ready to make an investment, technology options have expanded. According to[EHS Today](https://www.ehstoday.com/safety-technology/article/21154410/a-weighty-proposition-exoskeletons-in-the-workplace) , manufacturers such as Toyota, Ford and Boeing use devices called exoskeletons, which are hard mechanical frames with joints that let workers move more easily while reducing muscle strain. As the technology has become more practical and affordable, smaller manufacturers have started using it.


[Collaborative robots, or cobots](https://www.mscdirect.com/knowledge-center/articles/cobots-and-manufacturing-3-ways-collaborative-automation-can-help-your-shop) , are a similar step up. These tabletop robots can be programmed to handle repetitive, dirty or dangerous tasks, freeing workers for more satisfying roles.


## Building a Fatigue Risk-Management Plan for 24/7 Operations


A fatigue risk-management plan comes down to the two main levers that OSHA identifies in its[prevention guidance](https://www.osha.gov/worker-fatigue/prevention) : arranging schedules to allow rest breaks and adequate sleep, and adjusting the work environment—lighting, temperature, physical surroundings—to support alertness.


The American Academy of Sleep Medicine[recommends](https://aasm.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/ProviderFS-ShiftWork.pdf) limiting night shifts to blocks of three, using clockwise or forward rotation (day to evening to night), since it’s easier on the body’s circadian rhythm, and allowing three days of recovery after a stretch of nights before rotating back to days.


Simple environmental adjustments also help, such as brighter lighting during night shifts and scheduled short naps during circadian low points (typically the early morning and early afternoon hours).


Hazard reporting is part of a successful risk-management plan. Workers should have a direct way to flag fatigue and ergonomic concerns, with a clear expectation that supervisors respond quickly.


## Tracking Ergonomics and Fatigue Metrics Over Time


To know whether your interventions are working, track leading indicators—near-miss reports, worker-reported hazards, overtime hours and how consistently your schedules meet the fatigue-management limits above—alongside the lagging indicator you already have: MSD[DART incident rates](https://www.mscdirect.com/knowledge-center/articles/osha-dart-safety-rate-explained-and-how-calculate-it) .


Reviewing these metrics by shift—not just in aggregate—often reveals a real pattern.[One study of shift-scheduling data](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10098862/) at a Fortune 500 manufacturer found that the risk of a safety incident rose with each consecutive day shift worked, peaking on the fourth consecutive shift, while the pattern for night-shift crews followed a different curve entirely. That kind of shift-level detail gives plant managers a data-backed case for where to invest first.
